title: What's in Its Pockets (d20)
summary: A quick-reach loot table for any humanoid the party stops to search — most of it mundane, some of it asking a question the bearer can no longer answer.
body: A quick-reach loot table for any humanoid the party stops to search — most of it mundane, some of it asking a question the bearer can no longer answer.
1. Three copper coins and a smooth river stone, warm from body heat.
2. A folded letter, sealed but never sent, addressed to someone named "Mira."
3. Half a hardtack biscuit wrapped in a scrap of oilcloth.
4. A small knife, blade notched, handle wrapped in yellow cord.
5. Seven teeth. Not the bearer's.
6. A prayer token — wrong faith for this region.
7. A key on a cord, iron, unlabelled.
8. Two mismatched dice, both weighted the same way.
9. A scrap of map, edges burned, showing a coastline with an X.
10. A glass eye, brown, wrapped in soft cloth.
11. A pouch of dried herbs — culinary, harmless, and a long way from where they grow.
12. Twelve silver coins and one of pure gold, older-minted, the face unfamiliar.
13. A child's toy carved from bone. The cuts are fresh.
14. A folded wanted notice. The face on it is the party member who searched them.
15. A vial of dark liquid, stoppered tight, no label — not quite the same colour twice.
16. A small iron box, locked, no key. It is ticking.
17. A ring of hair woven tight, still on a severed finger.
18. A letter of safe passage, signed by someone who died three years ago.
19. A crude sketch of the nearest settlement — exits marked, guards noted.
20. Nothing. The pockets are sewn shut from the inside.

title: Coast & Tide Weather (d12)
special_element: Roll a 12 and the coast takes everything spoken for sixty seconds and hands it back at full volume. That makes the Hush a decision rather than a mood: hold your tongue for a minute, or let the sea repeat you to whoever is standing on the shingle. Warnings, plans, names, the price someone agreed to pay, the thing one player has been carefully not saying — the sea is not choosy and it does not paraphrase.
body: Category: Random Table · Biome: coast
Salt on the lips, gulls arguing overhead, the suck and slap of water working at the rock. The sea sets the mood of a shoreline scene before anyone at the table opens their mouth.
1. Flat calm. Glassy water, no wind. Sound carries too well — a conversation two hundred feet off comes across word for word.
2. Onshore breeze, cold. Salt spray stings any skin left bare.
3. Fog bank rolls in off the water. Visibility down to 30 feet inside ten minutes.
4. Warm rain, straight down, no wind. The sea stays glassy under it.
5. Squall line on the horizon, closing. Thirty minutes until it lands.
6. Low tide, further out than the oldest local has seen it. Wet sand stretching on and on.
7. Bioluminescent bloom. After dark, every wave breaks in cold blue light.
8. Dead low pressure. Ears pop. The gulls go quiet and settle on the water instead of flying.
9. Riptide — a flat, oddly smooth channel cutting out through the surf.
10. Heavy swell with no wind behind it. Boats roll at anchor with nothing pushing them.
11. Storm surge. Water climbs past the usual line, shoving wrack and driftwood inland.

12. **The Hush.** Every sound of the sea stops at once — wave, gull, current, above the surface and below it — for one full minute. Nothing said aloud in that minute makes any sound at all. Then the sea starts again, and the first wave to break gives the words back in the speaker's own voice, loud enough to carry the length of the shore.

Rows 1–11 are dressing. Use them to colour travel, set visibility, or tilt a scene's mood; none needs a ruling of its own. Row 12 is the one that bites. Run the minute close to real time: stop narrating, let the silence sit, and let the players choose whether to talk. Then read back what they said, verbatim, and let the shore hear it. Cost, when it lands: anything within earshot of the water learns what was said. Pursuers get a bearing, an NPC in the scene gets the secret, a negotiation gets the party's actual number. Verbal spell components fail inside the Hush and do not go off late — the words come back without the magic. The Hush needs no explanation and offers none. If you want one, decide privately what it is and hold that answer every time you roll it; the cost above works either way. Row 7 is ordinary sea-fire, not the cold light of the drownings further up the coast — say so at the table, unless you want it to be. Re-roll or reskin any row already contradicted by the scene; don't roll fog into weather you've described as clear.

Special element: Roll a 12 and the coast takes everything spoken for sixty seconds and hands it back at full volume. That makes the Hush a decision rather than a mood: hold your tongue for a minute, or let the sea repeat you to whoever is standing on the shingle. Warnings, plans, names, the price someone agreed to pay, the thing one player has been carefully not saying — the sea is not choosy and it does not paraphrase.

title: Forest Rumours (d10)
summary: Category: Table · Region: — · Biome: forest · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Table · Region: — · Biome: forest · Mood: mysterious

The camp cook stirs the pot without looking at it, listening instead to whoever just came in off the Red Stag Trail. Woodsmoke, wet wool, the fire popping. Half of what gets said around this fire turns out to be true, and nobody agrees on which half.
**d10 — roll or pick one:**

**The one special element:** before the session, roll d10 twice in secret. Those two rumours are the *same true thing*, seen from two sides — everything else on this table is wrong. Both truths sit in plain sight among eight lies, and the party has to spend to find out which. Chasing a false rumour costs a day in the woods (a night camped rough, one exhaustion check or one wandering-encounter roll, DM's call). Pressing the same local twice about the same false lead costs more than time: word gets round that strangers are asking, and whatever the true pair is about starts asking back. When the party finally chases one of the two real ones, tell them plainly that this one holds — and let them work out for themselves which other line on the list has been describing it all along.

**DM notes (do not read aloud):** the pair is the whole trick, so pick it deliberately if the dice give you a dull one — 5 and 9 make a circle that hunts by name; 2 and 4 make a table set for someone who came back; 1 and 7 make a wood quietly reorienting itself around one oak. Write the truth of the pair down in one sentence before play so you can't be talked out of it mid-scene. Recommended anchor is entry 10, which links to the Red Stag Trail's self-rearranging pull (`related: red-stag-trail`); entry 8 pays into the Stag's older bargain (`related: the-fey-bargain-of-the-stag`) if you want the fey reading. This table is *talk*, not events — nothing here happens to the party until they go looking for it, which is what separates it from a road-events table. Run it as a rumour-mill social scene, and let the eight lies stay lies; a wood where everything whispered turns out to be true isn't mysterious, it's just a quest board.
1. A woodcutter swears his axe keeps drifting toward one particular oak, no matter where he starts the swing.
2. Someone left a full dinner setting at the fork in the old trail — plates, cups, no chairs. Still warm this morning.
3. The trappers won't say why they stopped running lines past the third creek crossing. They just won't.
4. A girl walked out of the tree line three days ago in clothes two generations out of fashion. She hasn't aged a day since, by her own account.
5. Birdsong stops dead in a perfect circle somewhere past the ridge. The circle moves. It's always the same size.
6. A hunter found his own boot prints leading him back to his own camp — freshly made, before he'd walked that way at all.
7. The old shrine stones past the tree line have started facing a new direction. Nobody moved them.
8. A merchant paid in coin that turned to leaves by the time he got it home — and he swears he'd take it again.
9. Something out there answers to names it hasn't been told yet.
10. The Red Stag Trail took a farmhand somewhere he won't name, and he won't go near the trees again. Not fear, exactly. More like he's afraid of what he'd get if he asked twice.

title: Night-Market Wares (d20)
special_element: The stalls remember rolls, not faces. Roll the same result twice for the same character across visits and that stallholder opens with the secret paid last time — said back word for word, unprompted, before naming a price for anything else.
summary: Category: Random Table · Biome: urban · Tags below
body: Category: Random Table · Biome: urban · Tags below

Lantern-glass in a dozen colours, brine and hot wax on the air, and coins that vanish into a palm without ever being counted. Ask a stallholder for a price and they tilt their head, like they're listening for one instead.
Roll once per customer, or once per stall if the party is browsing together.
1. A compass that points at the thing you're most afraid of losing — costs the name of who you'd protect first.
2. A jar of bottled fog from a fight you survived — costs the detail of how you nearly didn't.
3. A single boot, worn through at the heel — costs the name of whoever's still looking for its owner.
4. A folding knife that never needs sharpening — costs a scar's true story.
5. Dried fish that tastes of somewhere you've never been — costs the place you're actually from.
6. A tin whistle that plays one note wrong — costs the tune you can't stop humming.
7. A rope that always coils clockwise — costs a promise you broke and never admitted.
8. A candle that burns silver-blue — costs the name of someone you'd rather forget.
9. A pair of dice, always warm — costs your worst bet, told in full.
10. A cracked mirror shard — costs what you saw in it once and never repeated.
11. A child's drawing, no child claims it — costs who you think drew it.
12. A key to a door that doesn't exist yet — costs what you hope is behind it.
13. A love letter, unsent, unsigned — costs the name it was meant for.
14. A vial of tears, sealed with wax — costs whose they were.
15. A map with one street missing — costs why you avoid that street.
16. A wedding ring, plain, still warm — costs whether you'd take it off if it were yours.
17. A deck of cards missing the ace of hearts — costs who has it now.
18. A bell that only rings for you — costs why you'd need warning.
19. A flask that's never empty, never full — costs the last thing you drank to forget.
20. Nothing on the table. The stallholder just watches, and asks what you're really here for.

Stock a Market of Quiet Coins scene from this table instead of inventing prices on the fly. Track rolled results per character across sessions if you want the callback; result 20 is the market testing whether a repeat customer will pay again. The cost is always information the character says out loud. Let the player decide how much they reveal, and let the stallholder lean in when they're specific. Never let a stall take coin instead. If a player insists, the item simply isn't for sale to them tonight.

Special element: The stalls remember rolls, not faces. Roll the same result twice for the same character across visits and that stallholder opens with the secret paid last time — said back word for word, unprompted, before naming a price for anything else.

title: Cavern Hazards (d8)
special_element: The cave answers noise. Keep a running tally of loud acts — combat, shouting, a forced door, a torch struck against stone. At three marks the next roll on this table lands one step worse than written. At five, results 6 and 8 stop being flavour: the echo is following them, and the breathing has a body — it takes the party's only clear exit and holds it, and they buy their way past with silence, with light, or with blood.
summary: Category: Random Table · Biome: cavern · Tier: 1–2
body: Category: Random Table · Biome: cavern · Tier: 1–2
Water ticks somewhere unseen. Stone-cold air pushes past in a slow draft, smelling of wet rock and old iron. Every footstep comes back a half-beat late — as if the dark listens before it answers.
1. A ceiling seam lets go — scree and fist-sized rock rattle down over a ten-foot spread.
2. A crevice underfoot is already flooding; cold water climbs past the ankles in seconds.
3. Bruise-blue fungus carpets the next passage; brushing it puffs numbing spores into the air.
4. A flowstone shelf, slick as glass, splits underfoot at the lip of a drop.
5. The air goes stale — torches gutter low, breath comes short, thinking comes slow.
6. Footsteps return wrong: two beats where there should be one, out of an empty passage.
7. A crystal vein hums at the pitch of a struck weapon, then shears into choking, glittering dust.
8. The draft dies. In the sudden quiet, something breathes that isn't the party.

Decide before play what the breathing thing in result 8 is, and what it wants: passage, quiet, or one of them. Pick one of the three and hold to it — the escalation only pays if the answer is already fixed when the fifth mark lands. Whatever you choose, it must be beatable without a fight. Dousing every light, splitting the party's noise between two passages, or surrendering the loudest thing they carry all count as paying the toll. Clear the tally only after a full turn of true silence — no torches struck, no arguing, no doors. Stopping the talking is not enough. On a repeat, vary the detail rather than reading the same line twice. The cave should not repeat itself. Mark noise openly at the table if you want the pressure felt; keep it hidden if you want the fifth mark to land cold.

Special element: The cave answers noise. Keep a running tally of loud acts — combat, shouting, a forced door, a torch struck against stone. At three marks the next roll on this table lands one step worse than written. At five, results 6 and 8 stop being flavour: the echo is following them, and the breathing has a body — it takes the party's only clear exit and holds it, and they buy their way past with silence, with light, or with blood.

title: Frontier Travel Events (d12)
special_element: Rows 3 and 11 are the same mark, re-cut closer each time the party passes. Three marks is the whole clock: the first claims a stretch of road, the second claims the road ahead of them, and the third is cut wherever the party finally stops — the gatepost of the town they were making for, the tree they tied the horses to. The night after the third notch, something takes one thing left outside the firelight and leaves three fresh cuts where it stood.
body: Category: Random Table · Biome: frontier

The road between settlements is long, empty, and never quite as empty as it looks. Cold ash where no fire should be. A bell somewhere with no tower under it. Tracks that turn to face you, then stop. Roll when a session needs a beat on the road.
1. An overturned cart blocks the track, one wheel still spinning. The horse is gone; the kettle on the cook-fire is still steaming.
2. A piper practices badly on a hilltop, out of tune and out of time. The moment anyone looks up, the sound stops.
3. A fence post is cut with three deep notches, the sap still wet — though no axe has touched this stretch in years.
4. A line of dogs crosses the road nose-to-tail, tails low, and will not set a paw past the mile-marker ahead.
5. A merchant caravan has camped early, guards doubled at midday. None of them will say why once the sun goes down.
6. A trail of coins runs off the road into the trees, one every twenty paces, newest-minted first.
7. An old woman sells water from a well that appears on no map. She won't take coin — only a name, given freely.
8. A standing stone lies freshly toppled. The grass crushed beneath it is bone-pale, as though it had lain there a hundred years by morning.
9. Birdsong cuts out along a quarter-mile stretch, then picks up again exactly where it stopped, mid-note.
10. A cairn of stacked stones sits warm to the touch on a morning cold enough to see your breath.
11. Another fence post bears three notches, cut fresh — the same hand, the same shape, a full day's travel nearer to wherever the party is going.
12. Riders pass the other way in total silence. Every one of them nods once, like they already know you.

Treat rows 3 and 11 as one motif, not two results, and keep a tally across trips: first notch, second notch, third. A second roll after the party has already seen the first means the mark has moved closer — it never resets, and it never appears further back. The third notch is the payoff, and it costs something specific. Pick the loss before it lands: a horse, a hireling's pack, the hireling. It goes cleanly and quietly, and the notches are cut where it was standing. Nothing is hurt on the road itself; the road is only where the counting happens. The party's out is the wet sap. While it's still running — half a day, no more — the cut can be backtracked off the road, and they get the meeting on their terms instead of at three. Leaving the road costs them the day's travel and whatever the day's travel was for. That's the choice: pay a day now, or pay the third notch later. Decide before play what cuts the marks — a scout, a fey, something that hasn't shown itself — but never answer it while the party is walking. The road doesn't explain; only the hunt does. The other ten rows are disposable colour and can repeat across trips without consequence. Row 1 in particular is nobody's story — the cart is abandoned, the kettle just hasn't cooled, and no one is coming back for either. Only the notches recur with meaning.

Special element: Rows 3 and 11 are the same mark, re-cut closer each time the party passes. Three marks is the whole clock: the first claims a stretch of road, the second claims the road ahead of them, and the third is cut wherever the party finally stops — the gatepost of the town they were making for, the tree they tied the horses to. The night after the third notch, something takes one thing left outside the firelight and leaves three fresh cuts where it stood.
